quoted_tweet.author: Andy Hall
quoted_tweet.text:
Frontier models can now propose technical social science research designs that experts grade more highly than the world's top political economist's---that's the finding from our new Free Systems eval, SnyderBench, in which we have PhD experts blind grade research proposals from AI models compared to papers written by Harvard political economist Jim Snyder (which the experts have not previously read). 

At the same time, we see no evidence that models can develop research ideas that experts rate as better overall contributions. They're getting better and better at the technical part of research, but not necessarily at the more subjective part.

This could be because human experts possess "judgment" that the models do not. 

It could also be that research "contribution" is so subjective that it doesn't actually point at any meaningful goal---consistent with this possibility, we find that our human experts don't agree with one another when rating project ideas for the strength of their contribution, with agreement rates barely higher than random chance. Perhaps social science research is what @alexolegimas might call a "relational good": something people value in part because it's produced by a human. We're not sure. 

This past January, I released the results of a pilot in which I had Claude Code replicate and extend a past empirical paper on vote-by-mail. 10 months later, it's stunning the amount of progress that's been made. It's no longer interesting to ask whether AI can collect data and run analyses automagically---we take that for granted---instead, the question is how much of the entire research loop AI can complete. Our tentative answer: AI can handle the technical aspects of empirical political economy research from end to end, devising the design and executing it, but for now, we still need humans to drive the agenda. 

This is joint work with @AndyCWMyers, and is of course dedicated to my PhD advisor Jim Snyder, who remains the world's great empirical political economist, AI or no AI. 

Lots more in the full piece here:

https://freesystems.substack.com/p/benchmarking-ais-research-taste-in

text:
You check every answer AI gives you, line by line.

5 prompts that make it check itself first, so you only read the version that passed.

Most bad answers don't come from a weak model. Nobody told it what done looks like, so it stops at the first draft that sounds right.

This week two posts promising "agents that fix their own mistakes" got 8,000+ bookmarks between them. You don't need an agent setup for that. You need the loop in plain text, and it works in ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini.

Prompt 1: Define done
"Before you start on [task], write 5 checks a finished answer must pass. Make each one specific enough that a stranger could mark it pass or fail, like 'every number has a source' or 'under 200 words'. Wait for me to approve the list."

Prompt 2: Plan before you write
"Write a short plan: the steps, what you need from me, and which check each step serves. If a check isn't covered by any step, add one. Then do the work."

Prompt 3: The strict reviewer
"Now switch roles. You're the toughest reviewer I know and you didn't write this. Grade the draft against each check: pass or fail, with the exact line that fails. No compliments."

Prompt 4: Fix and repeat
"Fix only what failed. Run the review again. Repeat until everything passes or you've done 3 rounds. If something still fails after 3, stop and tell me what's blocking it instead of guessing."

Prompt 5: Check against my ask
"Read my original request again. List anything I asked for that's missing or changed. Then show me only the final version and one line on what changed since the first draft."

Paste them into one chat, in order. The first run takes 5 minutes. After that, keep prompts 1 and 3 handy and you'll use them every day.

text:
You pay for fast internet and your Wi-Fi delivers a fraction of it. One prompt lets Claude or Codex find out why while you make coffee.

The usual culprit isn't your provider. It's a crowded channel, a slow DNS, or your laptop stuck on the 2.4 GHz band. Your router won't tell you. An agent that can use your computer can measure all of it.

Bruno Volpato tried it and posted his prompt. 4,000+ people saved it. His fixes: a faster DNS, cleaner channels and a separate 5 GHz network.

Here's our version. Run it in Claude Code, Codex or any agent that can use your terminal.

Prompt 1: Diagnose
"Diagnose my Wi-Fi and home network and find the real bottleneck. Run these one at a time, never two at once:
1) my Wi-Fi band, channel, channel width, signal and noise
2) a scan of nearby networks, counting how many share each channel
3) 30 pings to my router and 30 to 1.1.1.1 while nothing else is running
4) a short traceroute to separate home lag from provider lag
5) my current DNS and how fast it answers compared with 1.1.1.1 and 8.8.8.8
6) anything using bandwidth in the background
Explain each result in one plain line. Don't change any settings yet."

Prompt 2: Fix plan
"Rank the fixes by how much they'll help and how easy they are. For each one: what to change, where (router page or my computer), how to undo it, and how we'll measure the difference. Start with the top one and test again after each change."

No agent? Ask ChatGPT for the 3 commands for your system, run them yourself and paste the results back with Prompt 2.

The router setting nobody touches is usually the one slowing you down.

I'm excited to introduce Embo!

We are building the brain for intelligent robots to help people around the world.

We believe intelligent robots will unlock an era of abundance, making goods and services affordable for everybody. But to deploy them at scale, robots need to work out of the box in unfamiliar scenarios. At Embo, we are building frontier AI models with a deep understanding of physical reality and fine-grained motor skills.

Today's robot skills are fragile. Demonstrations can teach repetitive behaviors, but they cannot cover every object or situation a robot will encounter. We need general pretraining at internet scale to fill the gaps between individual tasks and practice to develop reliable motor skills.

The world models our team has pioneered unlock a path to general robots. Our robot brain pretrains on massive amounts of internet video to learn about objects, physical interactions, and how tasks unfold. It then practices motor skills in diverse imagined scenarios to become robust to unexpected situations.

Our team is behind seminal work in AI including Dreamer, VideoGPT, and Diffusion Forcing, with experience from DeepMind, Meta Superintelligence Labs, NVIDIA Cosmos, Berkeley, and MIT.

We have raised a $110M Seed led by @a16z. We are excited to partner with them, @khoslaventures, DST Global, NVentures (@nvidia), @strikervp,  and other strategic investors to bring reliable intelligent robots out into the world.

英伟达董事会让黄仁勋回来当 CEO，离他辞职只隔了 10 天

英伟达董事会 11 月 22 日宣布，全票通过恢复黄仁勋的总裁、CEO 和董事职务，即刻生效。11 月 12 日，他刚刚辞去这三个职务。董事会说，做决定前听取了美国政府高层的意见，认为他回来不会带来国家安全风险。

英伟达是全球最主要的 AI 芯片公司，ChatGPT 这类 AI 服务的训练和运行，大量依靠它的芯片。黄仁勋 1993 年和人合伙创办英伟达，之后一直担任 CEO（首席执行官，负责公司日常经营的最高负责人）。董事会是由股东选出、负责监督公司和任免 CEO 的一组人。

【他为什么离开】

按时间顺序：

1. 据维基百科汇总，《纽约时报》10 月 29 日最早报道：美国情报部门认为一名中国籍女子在为中国情报机构提供信息，黄仁勋是她接近的对象。这名女子曾是新加坡公司 Megaspeed 的高管。

2. 11 月 8 日，英伟达董事会宣布成立只由独立董事组成的委员会，调查黄仁勋成为"外国情报行动"目标的报道。独立董事指不在公司任职、和管理层没有利益关系的董事。同一天，黄仁勋给员工发信，承认有婚外情。

3. 11 月 11 日，《纽约时报》又报道，他和一名向他汇报工作的英伟达女高管有私人关系。

4. 11 月 12 日，英伟达宣布黄仁勋辞职，财务总监 Colette Kress 兼任临时 CEO。公告没有写辞职原因。

5. 11 月 17 日，黄仁勋在 X 上说自己在个人生活上犯了"严重错误"，如果董事会认为对股东有利，他愿意回来。同一天，董事长 Harvey Jones 在财报电话会上说，董事会不打算让他复职。

6. 11 月 18 日，据 CNBC 报道，Harvey Jones 在全员大会上说，董事会接受辞职是因为黄仁勋的个人行为和"不够坦诚"。

7. 据维基百科汇总，特朗普 11 月 20 日公开说希望黄仁勋能得到"第二次机会"。

【这次董事会做了什么】

公告说，董事会和黄仁勋多次面谈后，对他的坦诚和领导能力感到满意。具体安排是：

1. 黄仁勋恢复总裁、CEO 和董事职务。

2. Harvey Jones 继续当董事长。Colette Kress 不再兼任 CEO，继续当 CFO（首席财务官）。

3. 针对"外国情报行动"的独立调查继续进行到结束，委员会请了独立律师协助。黄仁勋表示支持并配合调查。

4. 董事会新设"国家安全与出口管制委员会"，也只由独立董事组成，负责监督贸易合规和国家安全风险。出口管制是美国政府限制先进芯片卖给某些国家（包括中国）的规定。

5. 公司开始招聘新设的首席合规官。这个职位负责检查全公司是否遵守法律法规，向董事会下属的提名与公司治理委员会汇报。

6. 英伟达继续配合政府正在进行的调查和问询。官方没说具体是哪些调查。据维基百科汇总，美国商务部和司法部 11 月 16 日的联合声明说，商务部从 2024 年起调查 Megaspeed，司法部已在主导一项刑事调查；英伟达 2025 年 6 月已把 Megaspeed 列入"不卖货"名单。

text:
Everyone's celebrating Jensen Huang's comeback today.

Stop reading the same media narrative that just hunted him down.

Look at what actually happened. And who won.

1. The $15B debt & 401(k) trap

Anthropic's operating loss was ~1.75× its revenue.

Affiliates of 16 of its 22 underwriting banks also arranged its $15B credit line.

Nasdaq bent its rules (15-day fast entry) to lock in ~$19B–$23B of forced passive 401(k) buying.

Right as Anthropic insiders unlock up to 316M shares on Day 1.

2. The ambush & tech betrayal

Oct. 26: Anthropic sends its IPO to the SEC.

During October's chip selloff, Nvidia barely flinched compared to the sector.
SMH -14.4%. Nvidia -9.7%.

Even a full week after the Oct. 29 "spy" stories dropped (alongside a Nov. 4 House chairs' letter, not a subpoena), the semiconductor index still fell more than Nvidia.
SMH -17.3%. Nvidia -15.9%.

So The New York Times swapped in the reporters who had just written a glowing Nov. 5 profile of Dario Amodei.

They published an executive-affair story without ever having seen the video.

Followed immediately by a sub-24-hour Wachtell probe pushing Huang out.

Meanwhile:
• This summer, Anthropic quit ITI, breaking with every other major U.S. tech company.
• OpenAI flipped the day Huang stepped down.
• Three chip-control bills were jammed into the Senate NDAA.

3. Lutnick used & dumped. Same table.

June: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick cites export-control criminal and civil penalties.
Sept.: "We trust Anthropic."
Nov. 13–15: The New York Times turns on him.
Nov. 19: his family firm Cantor Fitzgerald sits on Anthropic's IPO cover (4.9M shares + fees). The exact morning Commerce's BIS remote-access chip rule takes effect.

Already at the same table:
• Cantor: Tether's main U.S. Treasury custodian & 5% owner.
• Lutnick's children's Dynasty Trust A: borrowed from Tether.
• Continental Strategy: Anthropic's $740K lobbyist. Same lobbyist, Carlos Trujillo, registered for Tether.
• Wachtell: handled Lutnick's May 2025 Cantor handover.

4. Nov. 23: The jacket is back. The cage is permanent.

One weekend after Anthropic's Nov. 19 IPO, Nvidia's board cited "senior U.S. gov't input" clearing "no national security risk."

Three weeks of spy headlines. Erased overnight.

Yet Nvidia stopped shipping H200s to China. And welded four permanent chains:

• Harvey Jones keeps the newly created Board Chair seat.
• Wachtell's probe stays open.
• Barely four months after joining the expanded 11-seat board on July 13 (Audit Committee), 21-year Goldman Sachs veteran Suzanne Nora Johnson (Goldman led Anthropic's IPO) + Cooley's Stephen Neal (whose firm defended Anthropic in Bartz v. Anthropic) bypass the CEO to oversee exports and hire outside advisers.
• Nvidia is searching for a brand-new Chief Compliance Officer to oversee compliance across all of Nvidia. Bypassing Huang, the General Counsel, and the Audit Committee. Reporting straight to the Nominating & Corporate Governance Committee.

Now Jensen is back and the index rebounds.

Who actually wins?

Your 401(k)? No.

Your 401(k) just rode a rollercoaster so a booming tape could hand Anthropic's insiders (up to 316M unlocked shares) and 16 lender banks a smooth exit.

Right before Nasdaq forces ~$19B–$23B of automatic 401(k) buying.

The jacket is back. The cage is permanent.

Same bankers. Same lobbyists. Same law firm. Same calendar.

One beneficiary: Anthropic.

We're thrilled to invest in Embo.

Robots can already do remarkable things in demos, but those skills are fragile. Move an object, change the lighting, or introduce something unfamiliar, and the robot can struggle.

@EmboAI is building the brain for the humanoid workforce. They start by training a world model on massive amounts of video and robot demonstrations so that robots learn general knowledge far beyond what could be collected on their hardware.

Then an agent practices skills inside that model, trying different actions across imagined scenarios and improving through reinforcement learning. The world model provides physical knowledge, and practice turns that knowledge into skills.

Danijar Hafner and Wilson Yan have spent years developing world models together, and their work includes pioneering research like Dreamer and VideoGPT.

quoted_tweet.author: Danijar Hafner
quoted_tweet.text:
I'm excited to introduce Embo!

We are building the brain for intelligent robots to help people around the world.

We believe intelligent robots will unlock an era of abundance, making goods and services affordable for everybody. But to deploy them at scale, robots need to work out of the box in unfamiliar scenarios. At Embo, we are building frontier AI models with a deep understanding of physical reality and fine-grained motor skills.

Today's robot skills are fragile. Demonstrations can teach repetitive behaviors, but they cannot cover every object or situation a robot will encounter. We need general pretraining at internet scale to fill the gaps between individual tasks and practice to develop reliable motor skills.

The world models our team has pioneered unlock a path to general robots. Our robot brain pretrains on massive amounts of internet video to learn about objects, physical interactions, and how tasks unfold. It then practices motor skills in diverse imagined scenarios to become robust to unexpected situations.

Our team is behind seminal work in AI including Dreamer, VideoGPT, and Diffusion Forcing, with experience from DeepMind, Meta Superintelligence Labs, NVIDIA Cosmos, Berkeley, and MIT.

We have raised a $110M Seed led by @a16z. We are excited to partner with them, @khoslaventures, DST Global, NVentures (@nvidia), @strikervp,  and other strategic investors to bring reliable intelligent robots out into the world.

"What we really wanna do is bring something that is as good as Codex for coders, for scientists and to biotechs and pharma."

"When we are training GPT-Rosalind, we have all these interesting capabilities in the model in both chemistry and structural biology. We see that the models are doing really well on the benchmarks."

"But one repeated theme we've seen is that people don't know how to use the models. They don't know even what prompts to use, what questions to ask. What gets your product found, chosen, and bought by an AI agent?

a16z's Justine Moore and Olivia Moore partnered with The Prompting Company to test four consumer agents across 1,270 prompts and 11,307 completed runs.

Specific customer needs can overturn an agent's default recommendation. Shipping, returns, and seller credibility influence its choice. Requiring an account can stop it before checkout.

For businesses, winning an agent's business means making your product's value clear and giving the agent a path to actually buy or use it.

Full piece from a16z's Justine Moore and Olivia Moore: https://www.a16z.news/p/welcome-to-the-b2a-economy-how-agents

text:
Different AI agents send shoppers to different stores.

In The Prompting Company's tests, Instinct linked only to the brand's own store in 45% of answers, compared with 11% for Muse.

Muse included a retailer in 89% of answers, either alone or alongside the brand's store.

Like people, each agent has its own taste - which can impact what products an agent even considers, as well as what it ultimately selects.
